course_title: AI for Customer Experience and Support
overview: A three-week course for customer support, CX and operations teams who already work with customers. Learners see where AI helps in support, how AI assistants answer questions from a knowledge base, and why they sometimes give wrong answers. They design workflows that decide what AI should automate, what it should assist with, and what must stay with a person, with a clear hand-off to a human. No coding is needed: exercises use a free AI assistant, a free automation tool and a free chatbot builder. By the end, learners build a working support assistant prototype with a hand-off-to-human flow and a plan to measure it.

time_plan.per_week: About 20 minutes of video, 60 minutes of hands-on exercises, and 40 minutes of reading, quizzes and reflection. In week 3 the exercise time goes to building the capstone prototype.

objectives.text: Name the main ways AI is used in customer support: chatbots, ticket triage, agent assistance, knowledge bases and support analytics.
Explain how an AI assistant uses a knowledge base to answer questions, and why it can give wrong or invented answers.
Use a free AI assistant and automation tools to write knowledge base articles, draft replies in a consistent brand voice and automate simple support tasks.
Map a support workflow to decide which steps AI should automate, which it should assist with, and which must stay with a human, including hand-off triggers.
Evaluate an AI support assistant for accuracy, tone, response time, customer satisfaction, fairness and privacy.
Build a working support assistant prototype with a hand-off-to-human flow.

lessons.title: Where AI Helps in Customer Support
lessons.summary: Five common uses: chatbots, ticket triage, reply suggestions for agents, knowledge bases and analysis of customer feedback. The aim is faster answers without losing the human touch. Hypothetical examples include a telecom company in Morocco, an online shop in Vietnam and an airline in Mexico.
lessons.exercise: List the 10 questions your team receives most often and mark each one: AI can answer it, AI can help an agent, or a human must handle it.

lessons.title: How AI Assistants Answer Questions
lessons.summary: An AI assistant combines a language model with your own content, such as help articles and policies. Analogy: a new agent with a well-organised handbook gives good answers, but only if the handbook is correct and up to date. Without the right content, the assistant may invent an answer that sounds confident.
lessons.exercise: Ask Claude or ChatGPT a question about a made-up company's refund policy, first without and then with the policy text pasted in. Compare the two answers and note any invented details.

lessons.title: Writing a Knowledge Base That AI Can Use
lessons.summary: Good articles have one topic, a clear title, short steps, a review date and an owner. Content that is clear for customers is also clear for AI. Worked example: turning a long internal email about delivery delays in Nigeria into two short help articles.
lessons.exercise: Use an AI assistant to turn a messy internal note into 2 clean knowledge base articles. Check every fact against the original note.

lessons.title: Brand Voice and Reply Drafting
lessons.summary: A short tone guide helps AI draft replies that sound like your company, in several languages. Empathy, clarity and accuracy matter more than speed. An agent always reviews a draft before it is sent.
lessons.exercise: Write a 5-line tone guide, then use an AI assistant to draft replies to 3 upset customers. Edit each draft for accuracy and empathy and note what you changed.

lessons.title: Ticket Triage: Sorting and Routing with AI
lessons.summary: AI can label tickets by topic, urgency, language and sentiment, and send them to the right team. A wrong label can delay an urgent case, so categories must be clear and results must be checked. Worked example: a bank support team in Poland sorting tickets in three languages.
lessons.exercise: Define 5 ticket categories, then ask an AI assistant to classify 15 sample tickets. Compare its labels with your own and count the differences.

lessons.title: Mapping the Workflow: Automate, Assist or Human
lessons.summary: Four questions decide each step: How risky is a mistake? How emotional is the situation? How complex is the case? Could the customer be vulnerable? Worked example: mapping a refund request from first message to resolution.
lessons.exercise: Draw the workflow for one support process from your work and mark each step as automate, assist or human, with a reason.

lessons.title: Designing the Hand-off to a Human
lessons.summary: Hand-off triggers: the customer asks for a person, the assistant is unsure, the customer is very upset, the topic is sensitive (such as bereavement, fraud or health), or the same question fails twice. A good hand-off passes a short summary so the customer does not repeat the story. Analogy: a relay race, where the baton must be passed cleanly.
lessons.exercise: Write 5 hand-off rules and a hand-off summary template, then test the template on 2 sample conversations.

lessons.title: Automating Simple Tasks with n8n or Zapier
lessons.summary: A simple automation has three parts: a trigger, an AI step and an action. Worked example: a new contact-form message is labelled by AI and logged in a spreadsheet for the right team. Free plan limits and interface steps change often [VERSION].
lessons.exercise: Build a 3-step automation in n8n or Zapier's free tier that labels incoming form messages with AI and logs them in a sheet.

modules.title: Build, Test and Launch Your Assistant

lessons.title: Build Your Support Assistant
lessons.summary: Setting up an assistant in a free chatbot builder: choose its scope, add knowledge base content, write clear instructions and tell customers they are talking to AI. Keep the first version small: a few common topics done well. Interface steps are marked [VERSION].
lessons.exercise: Capstone step 1: build a support assistant in a free chatbot builder that answers questions on at least 3 topics from your knowledge base.

lessons.title: Adding the Hand-off Flow
lessons.summary: Connecting the hand-off rules from L07 to a real channel, such as an email, a ticket or a message to a team. The customer should know what happens next and when a person will reply. Worked example: an out-of-hours hand-off for a travel company in Kenya.
lessons.exercise: Capstone step 2: add a hand-off flow that sends the conversation summary to a human channel, using the builder's own feature or n8n or Zapier.

lessons.title: Testing Your Assistant: Accuracy, Tone and Safety
lessons.summary: A test set of about 20 questions, including tricky, out-of-scope, emotional and non-English questions. Score each answer for accuracy, tone and correct hand-off. Analogy: a driving test covers difficult roads, not only an empty car park.
lessons.exercise: Capstone step 3: run your test set, score each answer in a sheet, and fix the 3 biggest problems you find.

lessons.title: Measuring Success and Keeping the Human Touch
lessons.summary: Useful measures: first response time, resolution rate, hand-off rate and customer satisfaction. A high rate of conversations that never reach a human is not always good if customers give up. Privacy and transparency: tell customers when they talk to AI, and follow local data protection and disclosure rules [REGION] [VERIFY].
lessons.exercise: Capstone step 4: finish your prototype and write a one-page launch note with the measures you will track and the review schedule.

capstone.title: Support Assistant Prototype with Human Hand-off
capstone.brief: Build a working support assistant prototype with a hand-off-to-human flow.
